summary: Defines the default behavior of a BGP speaker when an External BGP session has no import or export policy. This avoids accidental route leaks that came from implementations accepting and advertising everything by default. It updates RFC 4271.

eli5.summary: If nobody gave rules about which messages to pass on, the router should pass none instead of everything.

questions: how to prevent bgp route leaks
subtitle: EBGP sessions should accept and send no routes until an operator configures policies.

tldr.problem: Many deployed BGP speakers accept and send all routes by default, so software defects or operator misconfiguration can cause route leaks.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds two rules to RFC 4271: without an explicit Import Policy, routes from an EBGP peer are not eligible in the Decision Process, and without an explicit Export Policy, routes are not added to the Adj-RIB-Out for that peer.
tldr.outcome: Operators must configure Import and Export Policies on every EBGP session, which gives consistent behavior across implementations and a safer default.

today: RFC 8212 is a Proposed Standard from July 2017 that updates RFC 4271. The metadata for this site shows no later RFC obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
BGP routing security needs attention to make the Internet more stable. Route leaks (RFC 7908) are part of the problem, and so are software defects and operator misconfiguration. RFC 8212 updates RFC 4271 so that routes are neither imported nor exported unless specifically enabled by configuration.

The RFC explains that many deployed BGP speakers send and accept any and all route announcements between neighbors by default. That practice dates back to the early days of the Internet, when operators were permissive so that all networks could reach each other. As the Internet became more densely interconnected, a misbehaving speaker poses significant risk.

The specification therefore requires explicit configuration of both Import and Export Policies for any External BGP (EBGP) session, such as customers, peers or confederation boundaries, for all enabled address families.
sections.eli5: It used to be fine for routers to trust everybody. Now the Internet is so tangled that one mistake can hurt many people, so routers should wait for instructions first.

sections.title: Import and Export Policies
sections.content:
RFC 4271 describes a Policy Information Base (PIB) holding local policies that apply to the Routing Information Base (RIB). RFC 8212 separates policies by where they apply.

Import Policy
A local policy applied to the information in the Adj-RIBs-In, which holds what was learned from other BGP speakers. Applying it produces the routes considered in the local Decision Process.
Export Policy
A local policy applied in selecting the information in the Adj-RIBs-Out, which holds what has been selected for advertisement to other BGP speakers.
sections.eli5: An import policy is the list of letters you will accept from a neighbor. An export policy is the list of letters you are willing to send to them.

sections.title: Changes to RFC 4271
sections.content:
When an EBGP session has no Import or Export Policy, two paragraphs added to RFC 4271 set the default.

In Section 9.1 (Decision Process), after the fifth paragraph, this is added: routes in an Adj-RIB-In associated with an EBGP peer SHALL NOT be considered eligible in the Decision Process if no explicit Import Policy has been applied.

In Section 9.1.3 (Phase 3: Route Dissemination), after the third paragraph, this is added: routes SHALL NOT be added to an Adj-RIB-Out associated with an EBGP peer if no explicit Export Policy has been applied.

A BGP speaker MAY provide a configuration option to deviate from these updated behaviors. The net effect is that a speaker following the specification does not use or send routes on EBGP sessions unless specifically configured to do so.
sections.eli5: Two simple rules: do not use anything a neighbor tells you until you have said what is okay, and do not tell a neighbor anything until you have said what is okay to share.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Permissive default policies can cause inadvertent effects such as route leaks, which generally send traffic through an unexpected path. An operator can use monitoring to spot unexpected flows, but the RFC notes there is no general framework for it. Permissive defaults can also expose software defects or misconfiguration with unforeseen technical and business impacts.

The update is meant to eliminate those inadvertent effects. Operators must explicitly configure Import and Export Policies to reach their goals. The RFC is clear about the limit: there is no protection against a malicious or incorrect explicit configuration.

The security considerations in RFC 4271 and the vulnerability analysis in RFC 4272 also apply. The RFC needs no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: This stops accidents, like a router sharing too much by mistake. It cannot stop someone who writes bad rules on purpose.

sections.title: Transition for Implementers
sections.content:
Appendix A is not normative. It says that moving to a compliant BGP implementation may take several years, and that operators who relied on undefined behavior will always be surprised when it changes.

It describes an 'N+1 and N+2' release strategy. In release N+1, the implementer adds a new default configuration parameter indicating the speaker runs in ebgp insecure-mode, and may start showing informational warnings that parts of the configuration are incomplete. In release N+2 or later, the inverse of that parameter becomes the default.

As a result, any new installation of release N+2 follows the RFC, while installations upgraded from N+1 keep the previous insecure behavior unless the ebgp insecure-mode parameter was changed.
sections.eli5: Software makers can change the rule slowly. First they warn everyone and add a switch, then in a later version they flip the switch to the safe setting for new setups.
